ambiguous.alternative: Integrity (or Confidentiality in a double-extortion case)
ambiguous.why: CC courseware treats ransomware as the canonical availability loss, but encrypting data in place also destroys its usable integrity, and modern ransomware exfiltrates first. The 'right' answer depends on the textbook framing rather than on the incident itself.

Backups are the classic availability control, but the word 'immutable' is an integrity property — write-once media primarily protects the backup from alteration, and only secondarily guarantees the data is reachable.

Signatures are an integrity control, so doctrine says OUT. The scenario, however, asks for records that survive 'intact', and a defensible reading is that a hospital cannot use restored records it cannot trust, making signatures part of the survivability story.

ambiguous.item: Keeping a tamper-evident audit log of who changed each record
ambiguous.alternative: Authentication (as the accountability half of IAAA)
ambiguous.why: Audit logging is normally taught under accountability/auditing in the IAAA chain rather than as non-repudiation proper; non-repudiation strictly requires cryptographic binding to an individual. Which bucket it lands in is a convention of the course material, not settled doctrine.

ambiguous.item: A code generated by an authenticator app on your phone
ambiguous.why: The factor is possession of the seeded device, which is the doctrinal answer. But the user demonstrates it by typing a value they read, and learners (and some study guides) argue the transcribed code behaves like knowledge.

ambiguous.item: Separation of duties on payment approvals
ambiguous.why: Separation of duties originates as a management/administrative decision, but in practice it is enforced by role configuration in the payments application, so it is frequently catalogued as a technical control.

ambiguous.item: A badge-operated turnstile in the lobby
ambiguous.why: The turnstile itself is physical, but badge-based access control is a hybrid: the underlying authorisation rules and issuance process are administrative, and some catalogues score the composite control that way.

assignment.A peer offers to sell you leaked ISC2 ex: Canon IV — advance and protect the profession
assignment.You publish your incident write-ups and: Canon IV — advance and protect the profession
assignment.You decline to exaggerate a threat in a: Canon II — act honourably, honestly, justly, responsibly and legally
assignment.A client pressures you to overstate thei: Canon II — act honourably, honestly, justly, responsibly and legally
assignment.You turn down a second client whose work: Canon III — provide diligent and competent service to principals
assignment.You tell a client up front that a specia: Canon III — provide diligent and competent service to principals
assignment.You report a vulnerability in a city's e: Canon I — protect society and the infrastructure
assignment.A vendor ignores your reports of a medic: Canon I — protect society and the infrastructure

ambiguous.item: A client pressures you to overstate their security posture in an audit report, and you refuse
ambiguous.my_answer: Canon II — act honourably, honestly, justly, responsibly and legally
ambiguous.alternative: Canon III — provide diligent and competent service to principals
ambiguous.why: Refusing to falsify a report is honesty (II), but the duty being exercised runs to a principal and Canon III explicitly covers rendering honest, candid service to the client. I changed my mind on this one.

ambiguous.item: You decline to exaggerate a threat in a sales pitch to frighten a prospect into buying
ambiguous.my_answer: Canon II — act honourably, honestly, justly, responsibly and legally
ambiguous.alternative: Canon IV — advance and protect the profession
ambiguous.why: FUD-based selling is dishonest (II), but ISC2's Canon IV guidance specifically warns against sensationalism and misrepresentation that damages the reputation of the profession.

ambiguous.item: You tell a client up front that a specialised cloud engagement is beyond what you are qualified to deliver
ambiguous.my_answer: Canon III — provide diligent and competent service to principals
ambiguous.alternative: Canon IV — advance and protect the profession
ambiguous.why: Canon III covers competent service to principals, but Canon IV's guidance says not to claim competencies you do not possess. The split depends on which canon's supporting guidance the writer had in mind.

ambiguous.item: You turn down a second client whose work would create a conflict of interest with your current engagement
ambiguous.my_answer: Canon III — provide diligent and competent service to principals
ambiguous.alternative: Canon II — act honourably, honestly, justly, responsibly and legally
ambiguous.why: Conflict-of-interest avoidance sits under Canon III's duty to principals in the ISC2 guidance, but it is equally readable as acting honourably and justly under Canon II.

ambiguous.item: Add a clause making the hosting provider financially responsible for data loss
ambiguous.why: Contractual indemnity is the textbook example of transfer, yet newer frameworks (and ISO 31000 language) call this 'sharing' because the organisation retains the operational and reputational loss and only moves the financial component.

ambiguous.item: All production servers must run the approved hardened OS image
ambiguous.why: It names a specific mandatory technical baseline, which is a standard. But phrased as a broad organisation-wide 'must' with no version or parameter, it also reads as a policy statement that a separate build standard would implement.

ambiguous.item: Safeguarding client information is a responsibility of every employee, at every level
ambiguous.why: It is a high-level intent statement, hence policy, but it is non-specific and unenforceable as written, and some courseware files aspirational statements of this shape as guidance rather than as binding policy.
